dossier.mechanism: Drop any file into one window; MediaKit reads its format and opens the right one of 152 local tools (video, audio, image, PDF, archive, ebook), running it on-device through Apple frameworks (AVFoundation, CoreImage, PDFKit, Vision, Speech, Compression), so the file never leaves the iPhone or Mac.
dossier.audienceScene: A Mac or iPhone owner in the middle of a task with a file that will not fit or will not open: a 55 MB screen recording too big to send, a HEIC a parent cannot open, two PDFs to merge, a RAR v5 from a client. They have just searched 'compress mp4 without uploading' or 'HandBrake alternative' and arrive on a phone or laptop, deciding in seconds.
dossier.culturalHome: Indie Mac-utility culture (menu-bar apps, Shortcuts, Apple Silicon) meets everyday media handling. Before the web, this job belonged to the photo-lab counter, the dubbing deck and the broadcast machine room. Today the upload-to-a-website converters (CloudConvert, Zamzar, iLovePDF) have taken it over, and the developer's own essays argue against them.
dossier.mustProve: One native app handles every format and picks the right tool itself. The file never leaves the device, shown through the transparency record rather than claimed. It is free to start: a 3-day full trial, five tools free forever, Pro from $3.99/mo. The official App Store badge (opening the Mac App Store on a Mac) and, on desktop, the QR for the iPhone must sit within reach.
dossier.categoryDefault: The converter page: a giant dashed 'Drop file here / Upload' box over a grid of MP4-to-MOV format pills on a purple gradient (CloudConvert, Convertio). The other default is the Mac-utility page: a centred icon over a big dark window screenshot, then a feature-card grid and a three-tier pricing table (Permute, HandBrake sites).
dossier.predictableOpposite: A stark white 'privacy' page (padlock, one sentence, acres of whitespace), or a terminal/ffmpeg command-line costume (the dev-tool rut).
dossier.literalReading: 'Media kit' read literally gives a toolbox, a Swiss-army knife or a workshop shadow board of tools (or a press-kit folder). Only candidate 7 uses it.
evidence: Front matter: 152 tools; 5 free forever (Video Compress, Image Compress, Image Resize, Audio Convert, PDF Compress); 147 behind Pro plus batch processing; 21 export presets; 6 Shortcuts actions; menu-bar access; iOS 17+ and macOS 14+; Universal Purchase; status live; App Store id 6761451361.

price.value: 'Free trial — Pro from $3.99/mo, $22.99/yr, or $39.99 lifetime'. Four plans: Free trial $0, Pro Monthly $3.99/mo, Pro Annual $22.99/yr (highlight: true), Lifetime $39.99 once ('Best long-term value'). Also has plans_footnote.

Blocks present: hero (device: mac), quick_answer, value_points (4), features (6), who_for (5), who_not_for (3), plans (4), screenshots (8, Mac landscape 3584x2130), privacy notes (5), faq (7), alternatives_to (16). ABSENT: founder, how_it_works (so no HowTo schema), comparison_table, roadmap, spotlight, training_vocabulary, insight_gallery, related_journal, testimonials, ratings; no iPhone screenshots exist.

App UI palette (screenshots): near-black navy ground tinted per tool family (blue-violet for Trim/GIF, purple for audio Convert, ember-brown for PDF, green for ZIP compress). Coral-pink primary 'Run' button, periwinkle-blue accent, small mono metadata pills (MOV · 55,3 MB · 0:42 · 1920×1080 · 30 fps). Signature result screen: 'Before 55,3 MB → After 42,7 MB, 22% smaller'. Drop zone reads 'Drop any media file · video · audio · image · PDF · archive · ebook'. The tool picker has category tabs All/Recipes/Video/Audio/Image/Pdf/Archive/Ebook.
Icon: three brushed-steel monolith bars with etched circuit lines, blue backlight, on a deep navy squircle.

Transparency (_data/transparency.yml): network calls none; data leaves device: no; analytics none; account none; permission: user-selected file only. third_party_sdks: 1 (Unrar.swift, open-source read-only RAR, no network). So the shared trust fact '0 third-party SDKs' would be FALSE here.

Alternatives: 14 pages target MediaKit (handbrake, cloudconvert, convertio, permute, adapter, wondershare-uniconverter, hitpaw-video-converter, imazing-heic-converter, xnconvert, izip, compress-videos-resize-video, image-size, pdf-expert, documents-by-readdle). Keka and ImageOptim are in alternatives_to with no page. The pages already concede honest trade-offs (HandBrake: 'Equally on-device', deeper encoder tuning).

Journal: 'The Mac already shipped with every media tool — someone just had to wire them together' (the bet is consolidation, not novelty). 'Your photos shouldn't ride the elevator to a stranger's data centre' (the six steps an uploaded file takes: leaves, lands on operator storage, processed, held hours or days, downloaded, maybe deleted).

Drift to respect: both journal posts say 133 tools and 'one-time Pro, no subscription', and screenshot 1 shows '129 tools'. Front matter (152; monthly/annual/lifetime) is authoritative for the microsite.

candidates.name: Transit network diagram: your device is Zone 1
candidates.why: Everyone reads a metro map by heart, and routing a file to its tool is literally wayfinding. Five coloured lines (one per format family, coloured from the app's own per-family tints) leave one interchange called Drop, and every station is a real tool. Chained tools become interchanges. The whole network sits inside a fare-zone boundary labelled 'your iPhone or Mac', while the cloud converters' route runs outside it, unconnected.

candidates.name: Mailroom sorting frame
candidates.why: Pigeonhole frames in offices, hotels and schools are known by sight. Every incoming item is read by its label and slotted into the right hole, which is exactly 'drop a file, it picks the tool'. The 152 holes carry brass label holders, and the ritual's own phrase ('internal post: never leaves the building') carries on-device.

candidates.name: Photo-lab drop-off envelope and counter
candidates.why: This is the pre-web counter where media got converted. You ticked film type, size and finish on a printed envelope, the clerk picked the process, and you kept a perforated claim stub. Labs also offered 'send out' for work they could not do in-house, which maps exactly onto cloud versus on-device. Here FILE TYPE ticks route to tools, 'Send out' is printed and struck through, and the claim stub is the download.

candidates.name: Department-store lift-lobby directory
candidates.why: 'Every department under one roof' is 'every tool in one app'. The changeable-letter lobby board lists floors (Video, Audio, Image, PDF, Archive, Ebook) with their departments (tools). The lift panel's buttons become navigation. It lifts the developer's own 'your photos shouldn't ride the elevator' essay: this lift has no button for the cloud.

candidates.name: Broadcast machine-room rack
candidates.why: Before software, each conversion was its own box in a 19-inch rack: a standards converter, a loudness processor, a format router. MediaKit is the whole rack in one app. The rack's units stack in scroll order, silkscreened panels carry the real 'broadcast-grade / EBU R128 / ProRes' claims, and the brushed-steel, navy-backlit icon is already this material.

candidates.name: Home darkroom under safelight
candidates.why: People built home darkrooms so no lab would see their pictures, which is the deepest form of the privacy promise. Trays, timer and easel can stage drop, process and done. It carries on-device strongly, but carries the breadth (PDF, archive, audio) weakly.

candidates.name: Workshop shadow board (literal 'kit')
candidates.why: A pegboard where every tool has its painted outline shows breadth and order at a glance. The five free-forever tools would be painted in a different colour. It is the literal reading of the name, so it is spent here and nowhere else, and it carries routing only by 'everything has its place'.

styles.label: Processed In-House
styles.lineage: The 1980s–2000s one-hour photo minilab counter: the printed drop-off envelope (FILM TYPE / SIZE / FINISH / SETS / SERVICE: 1-hour, next day, send out), its perforated claim-check stub, the backlit price board above the counter, the index print and the print wallet that came back.
styles.thesis: The page is the drop-off envelope of a lab that never sends anything out. 'Send out' is printed and then struck through, and ticking a file type routes it to its tools. It refuses the converter category's dashed upload box and its format-pill grid.
styles.scene: A Mac or iPhone owner at a bright desk in daytime with a file too big to send, reading the page the way you read an order form handed across a lit retail counter. So the scheme is light.
styles.colorStrategy: Drenched: the ground IS the envelope's flood-printed process-cyan stock edge to edge. Form panels are knocked out to white. All type on cyan is black ink, and one magenta 'second ink' is reserved for ticks, rings and the in-house stamp.

Sofia Sans 400/600 is the plain typed fill-in voice for reading copy, and the Condensed cut sets form labels. One superfamily works like a lab's matched stationery set. Four files total about 63 KB.

styles.navigation: The envelope's top flap is the nav: 'File types · Tool index · Price list · Questions · Privacy' set as printed tab labels, with 'Download free' at the right. The current section is underlined in magenta. On mobile, 'Menu' is a details/summary that folds down like the flap, with the same five links at 44px rows.
styles.signatureInteraction: Name: 'Tick the file type'. Technique: the FILE TYPE row is a real radio group. Ticking one, via CSS :has(:checked) with no JS, draws the magenta tick, re-inks the PROCESS and PRESETS rows for that type, and moves the in-house stamp onto it. JS enhancement: drop a real file onto the envelope (or 'Choose a file' on phones). The browser reads only file.name, ticks the matching type ('.HEIC → Image') and prints 'Nothing left this page — only the file name was read'. No-JS fallback: the Video row is pre-ticked and every type's full tool list is printed statically in the Index print below, so no content depends on the control. Reduced motion: the stamp and tick appear instantly, with no press.
styles.motionGrammar: Paper does not animate; ink lands. On a tick, the stamp presses (scale 1.04 to 1 with an opacity fade, 120ms ease-out) and the tick draws in 90ms. The sticky stub rises 8px over 160ms. Perforations, prints and sections never move or scroll-reveal. Under prefers-reduced-motion every state change is instant.
styles.readModeVariant: Privacy, support and alternatives pages wear the envelope's back. A 72px cyan flap band carries the page title in Extra Condensed 900 ink, and a 24px cyan strip runs down each margin. The reading column is a white knock-out at 66ch in Sofia Sans 18px/1.6 ink. The privacy policy's sections are printed terms headed in Condensed 600, followed by a ruled 'Lab use only' box of transparency facts. Support is a counter slip that lists, as empty tick boxes, what to include (device, OS version, file type, what happened), with the email address. Alternatives pages set the head-to-head as a two-column ruled order form ('MediaKit | HandBrake'), 'Pick MediaKit if…' as ticked boxes and 'Stick with HandBrake if…' as empty boxes, then FAQ open, ending with the perforated claim stub.
styles.assetsNeeded: None required: stock, rules, perforations and the stamp are CSS/SVG, and prints are cropped from existing screenshots. Optional: portrait iPhone screenshots of MediaKit (none exist) for one iPhone print in the wallet, and a _data/mediakit_tools.yml with all 152 tool names by type so the index print can be complete and frame-numbered.
styles.risk: It leans on a ritual many visitors under 30 never did, and the cyan drench with condensed caps could tip into retro pastiche or risograph-zine trend. The photo-lab frame may read as 'a photo app' unless all six file types are visible in the first viewport. The order form's density has to stay legible at 390px.
styles.memoryTest: 'It was a cyan photo-lab envelope where Send out was printed and crossed out. I ticked Video and it listed the tools, and the download button was the claim-check stub.'

styles.label: Zone One Network
styles.lineage: The schematic metro diagram: Harry Beck's 1933 Underground diagram and Vignelli's 1972 New York map (octilinear lines, ticks for stations, rings for interchanges), fare-zone maps with shaded zone boundaries, and the in-car strip map that unrolls one line vertically.
styles.thesis: MediaKit's routing drawn as a working network. Five lines in the app's own per-family colours leave one interchange called Drop, and every station is a real tool. The whole network sits inside a dashed Zone 1 boundary marked 'your iPhone or Mac', and the cloud converters' route runs outside it, never connected. It refuses the converter's upload box and the utility page's feature-card grid.
styles.scene: Someone mid-errand reading a station's network map on a white enamel panel under bright platform light: glanceable, coloured lines, black type. So the scheme is light.
styles.colorStrategy: Full palette: five named line colours (Video, Audio, Image, Documents, Archive), taken from the app's own per-family tints, run on white enamel with black type. Zone 1 is filled with ink at 6% over the ground, and the cloud route is ink-grey dashed. Colour only ever means 'which line'.

type.display: Overpass 800 (headline, line names), 600 (station names on the map)
type.utility: Overpass 800 tabular figures in the line roundels and fare table
type.rationale: Overpass is the open revival of Highway Gothic, the FHWA sign alphabet. These are the most-read wayfinding letterforms in North America, so headings and line names read as enamel signage. Atkinson Hyperlegible Next was drawn for the Braille Institute to keep letters and figures apart, which matters on a map full of 'OCR', 'EXIF', 'RAR v5', 'AES-256' and 'R128'. Four files total about 60 KB.

styles.navigation: The line legend is the navigation. Five roundels (V Video, A Audio, I Image, D Documents, Z Archive) jump to their line sections, followed by 'Fares', 'Questions' and 'Download free'. The current line's roundel gains an ink ring. On mobile, 'Lines' opens a details panel listing the roundels and named links at 44px rows. Sub-pages use a breadcrumb drawn as a short ink line with stops (Lagerland → MediaKit → Privacy).
styles.signatureInteraction: Name: 'Drop at Drop'. Technique: the Drop interchange is a real drop target, with a 'Choose a file' input on touch. JS reads only file.name (never the contents) and maps the extension using the FAQ's format lists. The matching line stays in full colour while the other four fade to 20% ink, and a departure-board line prints 'IMG_0937.HEIC → Image line: Convert · Compress · Resize · Strip EXIF · OCR', then 'Only the file name was read. Nothing left this page.' Without JS, hovering or focusing a legend roundel isolates its line with CSS :has(). Format chips (MP4 MOV MKV · MP3 FLAC WAV · HEIC RAW PNG · PDF EPUB · ZIP RAR) are plain links to each line section. No-JS fallback: the full static map with every line and station visible. Reduced motion: the line isolation switches instantly, with no line-draw.
styles.motionGrammar: Lines draw once on first load (stroke-dashoffset, 700ms ease-out-quart, staggered 80ms per line), but only under html.js, so the map is fully drawn without JS. Isolation crossfades over 180ms, the departure line types in over 240ms, and the sticky next-station bar slides up 160ms. Sections never reveal on scroll. prefers-reduced-motion turns everything off.
styles.readModeVariant: Privacy, support and alternatives pages become station information pages. A route-bar breadcrumb runs across the top (an ink line with stops Lagerland → MediaKit → this page), and the title is set in Overpass 800 on white enamel. The reading column is Atkinson 18px/1.6 ink at 66ch, with tables set as timetables. The privacy policy's sections become stops on a vertical ink contents line (Overview → Data collection → Storage → Third parties → Children → Changes → Contact), with a 'Network facts' table of transparency data. Support is a 'Help point' panel with the email address and a stop-list of what to include. Alternatives pages draw a two-line comparison strip ('MediaKit network: five lines' vs the competitor's single grey line, labelled only with facts from the page), then the comparison as a timetable, 'Pick MediaKit if…' and 'Stick with HandBrake if…' as two strip lists, FAQ, and the Fares box.
styles.assetsNeeded: None required: the diagram is hand-placed inline SVG built from front-matter tool names, and the screenshots exist. Strongly recommended: a _data/mediakit_tools.yml with all 152 tool names by family, so every line can show its full station list and not only the tools named in features and screenshots. Optional: portrait iPhone screenshots for the strip-map sections.
styles.risk: This is the most familiar strong idea: 'a subway map of X' is a well-worn explainer trope, and it is where many runs would land. It only earns its place if stations are working links and the legend really is the navigation, not a poster. The octilinear SVG has to be laid out by hand once and maintained when tools change. On phones the network collapses to strip maps, so the whole-network view is a desktop-first moment. Station lists stay partial until the full tool catalogue exists.
styles.memoryTest: 'A white metro map where every station was a tool. Five coloured lines met at Drop, all inside a dashed Zone 1 that said your iPhone or Mac, and the cloud converters' line sat outside it, never connected.'

styles.label: The Whole Rack
styles.lineage: The broadcast master-control machine room: the 19-inch EIA-310 equipment rack (1U = 1.75in) with rack ears and oval screw slots, silkscreened front panels of standards converters and loudness processors, jewel pilot lamps, rotary input selectors and rack-mount confidence monitors. Every format conversion used to be its own box here.
styles.thesis: Every conversion used to be a separate box bolted into a rack. The page is one rack seen from the front, where every box is a module of the same app, stacked unit by unit as you scroll. It refuses both the converter's upload box and the Mac-utility page's icon-over-screenshot.
styles.scene: A video editor or podcaster in a dim edit suite at night, the room lit only by the Mac screen and the rack's pilot lamps. So the scheme is dark.
styles.colorStrategy: Committed: deep blue-anodised aluminium (the icon's navy-steel) covers about 60% of the surface as module faceplates, framed by black rack rails. White silkscreen sets all type, and amber and green pilot-lamp jewels are the only saturated marks, each with a job: amber means selected or active, green means on-device or free. There is no glow anywhere.

type.utility: B612 Mono 400 (real readouts only: 55.3 MB → 42.7 MB, 0:42, 1920×1080, 152, 21, 6, prices in the plan rows)
type.rationale: Michroma revives Microgramma Extended, the wide capitals silkscreened onto 1970s–80s broadcast and studio rack panels. Its single weight is right for silkscreen, where legends have one ink weight. Barlow is a low-contrast industrial grotesk drawn from California plates and highway signs, and it reads as the operator's manual on dark at 17px. B612 Mono was drawn for Airbus cockpit displays, and it appears only where a real figure is read out. Four files total about 81 KB.

styles.navigation: The 1U nav module carries push-button legends: Input, Processors, Price, Manual (FAQ), Privacy, and 'Download free'. An amber pilot lamp lights beside the section in view, using IntersectionObserver, and the static first item is lit without JS. On mobile, 'Menu' opens a details panel styled as the rack's unit index, listing every module with its U position.
styles.signatureInteraction: Name: 'Input selector'. Technique: a five-detent rotary knob that is a real radio group (arrow keys move detents). With CSS only (:has(:checked)), selecting a detent turns the knob, lights that lamp amber, and switches the Output monitor to that processor's real screenshot. JS enhancement: drop a real file into the engraved well (or 'Choose a file' on phones). The browser reads only file.name and file.size, sets the knob from the extension, and prints 'IN: IMG_0937.MOV · 55.3 MB → Video processor · read in your browser only' in B612 Mono. No-JS fallback: the Video detent is pre-selected, every processor module below shows its own screenshot and tools, and nothing depends on the knob. Reduced motion: the knob jumps to the detent and the lamp switches without the 80ms fade.
styles.motionGrammar: Hardware-literal and terse. The knob rotates 30° per detent over 140ms (ease-out-quart), lamps switch on in 80ms with no glow or bloom, the monitor crossfades in 100ms, and the sticky 1U strip slides up over 160ms. Modules are bolted in: no scroll reveals and no parallax. Under prefers-reduced-motion all states are instant.
styles.readModeVariant: On privacy, support and alternatives pages the rack frame stays: rails with screw slots in the margins, a 1U legend strip at the top with the page title in Michroma, and a serial plate at the foot. The reading column is one manual-page module: Barlow 17px/1.65 #EEF2F7 on #12203F at 66ch, headings in Michroma 22px, and tables set as spec plates with B612 Mono used only for figures. The privacy policy's sections are manual chapters, with a spec-plate table of transparency facts. Support is a 'service request' module with the email address and a lamp-bulleted list of what to include. Alternatives pages set the comparison as a spec sheet (rows: scope, encoder depth, platform, privacy; columns: MediaKit | HandBrake), 'Pick MediaKit if…' with green lamps and 'Stick with HandBrake if…' with amber lamps, then the FAQ and the Output module with the badge.
styles.assetsNeeded: None required: rails, anodise grain, lamps and the knob are CSS/SVG, and the monitors show existing Mac screenshots. Optional: portrait iPhone screenshots of MediaKit, so one monitor can show the iPhone app, and the _data/mediakit_tools.yml catalogue for complete front-panel tool legends.
styles.risk: A skeuomorphic hardware rack can tip into costume or dated pastiche. Dark navy with amber lamps sits one step from the 'near-black plus one accent' cluster, so the anodise must stay visibly blue and the lamps flat. Michroma is very wide: headlines drop to 26px on phones and long words need care. Consumer visitors may not know a broadcast rack, so the idea leans on the visible 'every box in one' reading rather than recognition.
styles.memoryTest: 'The page was one blue equipment rack. Every tool was a module bolted in as I scrolled, I turned a knob to Audio and the monitor changed, and the download sat in its own Output panel next to a green Network: none lamp.'

canon: Canon (the standing exit, played straight): the dark Mac-utility product page, with a centred app icon and headline over a large Mac window screenshot on a deep gradient, a 'Download on the App Store' badge with a QR beside it, a row of format/feature cards, a three-column pricing table, an FAQ accordion and a footer, in the Permute / CleanShot register.
notes: Roll: key f577b333, degraded (no catalog challengers, no network retry by instruction). The assigned index is 3. Reroll 1 also landed on 3, so reroll 2 was used and gave 5. Rerolls 3 (4) and 4 (7) were printed in the same command but not used. Neither 3 nor 5 is candidate 1, so Style B is IMPECCABLE’S PICK (candidate 1); A = 3 (THE ROLL), C = 5 (SECOND ROLL). The seven-candidate order was locked before the roll. Factual guardrails for whichever style ships: (1) MediaKit declares 1 third-party SDK (Unrar.swift, open-source, read-only RAR, no network), so the shared '0 third-party SDKs' trust fact must not be shown for this app; say '1 open-source library, no network'. (2) No how_it_works in front matter means no HowTo schema; none of the styles invents steps. If the owner wants HowTo, add how_it_works (e.g. Drop → Pick → Save) to _apps/mediakit.md first. (3) No founder block, so the maker/freshness line only. (4) No iPhone screenshots exist although platforms include iOS; every style works on the 8 Mac screenshots, and iPhone shots are an optional production task. (5) Drift: both journal posts say 133 tools and 'one-time Pro, no subscription', and screenshot 1 shows '129 tools', while front matter says 152 tools and monthly/annual/lifetime. The microsite renders front matter only, captions must not quote the 129, and the owner should refresh the posts. The HandBrake alternatives page also mentions AV1, which is not in front matter, so it needs checking before it is reused in any comparison. (6) alternatives_to lists 16 names but only 14 pages exist (Keka and ImageOptim have none); render those two as plain text. (7) On a Mac desktop the badge opens the Mac App Store directly, so the QR is secondary and explicitly 'for your iPhone'. (8) All three signatures read only file.name (C also file.size) in the browser, never contents, and say so; that demonstration is itself proof of 'nothing uploaded'. (9) A shared content task would help every style: _data/mediakit_tools.yml listing all 152 tool names by family (data, not art).
